trial_name: PRORATA — Procalcitonin to Reduce Patients' Exposure to Antibiotics in Intensive Care Units (2010)
citation: Bouadma L, Luyt C-E, Tubach F, et al. Use of procalcitonin to reduce patients' exposure to antibiotics in intensive care units (PRORATA trial): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2010;375(9713):463-474.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, open-label, parallel-group, superiority (antibiotic exposure) and non-inferiority (mortality)
one_liner: A daily procalcitonin-guided algorithm reduced ICU antibiotic duration by 3 days without compromising 28-day survival, though clinician overrides were frequent and 60-day mortality point estimates numerically favored standard care.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients in France with suspected bacterial infection prompting systemic antibiotics and an expected ICU stay >3 days (n=621 analyzed).
pico.intervention: Procalcitonin (PCT)-guided strategy with daily PCT measurements informing antibiotic initiation (<0.25 µg/L strongly discouraged to ≥1 µg/L strongly encouraged) and discontinuation (stop if <0.25 µg/L or dropped ≥80% from peak).
pico.comparison: Standard-care antibiotic management based on contemporary guidelines and clinical judgement, with PCT levels masked to clinicians.
pico.outcome: Co-primary: Superiority for days without antibiotics (days 1–28) and non-inferiority for all-cause mortality at 28 days (10% non-inferiority margin, 90% CI).

background.existing_knowledge: ICU patients experience high empiric antibiotic exposure, driving antimicrobial resistance, drug toxicity, Clostridioides difficile infection, and resistant organisms. Routine clinical signs and CRP are non-specific, causing delayed discontinuation.
background.knowledge_gap: Evidence for PCT-guided stewardship in ICU was limited by small trials, heterogeneous algorithms/assays, and uncertainty regarding mortality non-inferiority.
background.hypothesis: A PCT-guided strategy reduces antibiotic exposure (increases antibiotic-free days) in ICU patients with suspected bacterial infection while remaining non-inferior for 28-day and 60-day mortality.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, controlled, parallel-group, open-label, investigator-initiated trial across 7 French ICUs, stratified by centre with variable block sizes; blinded expert adjudication of infectious outcomes.
methods.setting: 7 adult ICUs in France; enrolled at ICU admission or during stay upon new suspected infection.

inclusion: Suspected bacterial infection prompting consideration of systemic antibiotics
exclusion: Receipt of antibiotics for >24 hours before eligibility assessment
Anticipated need for long-term antibiotic therapy

methods.intervention: PCT measured at suspicion and daily during therapy with turnaround ~2 hours. Initiation guidance: <0.25 µg/L strongly discouraged, 0.25–<0.5 discouraged, 0.5–<1 encouraged, ≥1 strongly encouraged. Continuation/discontinuation guidance: stop strongly encouraged if <0.25 µg/L; stop encouraged if 0.25–<0.5 µg/L or decreased by ≥80% from peak; continuation encouraged if ≥0.5 µg/L with drop <80%; change antibiotics strongly encouraged if PCT increased vs peak and remained ≥0.5 µg/L. Clinical overrides permitted for severe syndromes (e.g. septic shock, meningitis) or ongoing clinical instability.
methods.comparison: Standard-care antibiotic management based on contemporary guidelines and clinician judgement without access to PCT values.
methods.blinding: Open-label for treating clinicians and patients; expert adjudication committee was blinded to allocation when confirming relapse and superinfection.
methods.sample_size_power: 133 patients/group for 3-day increase in antibiotic-free days (assumed mean 12, SD 7.5; 90% power, alpha 0.05); 300 patients/group to exclude 10% absolute mortality difference (assumed 35% mortality; 80% power, two-sided 90% CI). Planned enrolment 630.
methods.primary_outcome: Co-primary: Days without antibiotics through day 28 (superiority) and all-cause mortality at day 28 (non-inferiority, 10% absolute margin).
secondary_outcomes: Total antibiotic exposure (days of therapy, days 1–28)
methods.follow_up: Antibiotic exposure and infectious outcomes through day 28; mortality assessed at day 28 and day 60.

headline_bullets: PCT guidance increased antibiotic-free days by 2.7 days (14.3 vs 11.6 days, P<0.0001) and reduced overall antibiotic therapy by 3.0 days (10.3 vs 13.3 days, P<0.0001).
Day 28 all-cause mortality met non-inferiority criteria (21.2% vs 20.4%, difference 0.8%, 90% CI -4.6 to 6.2).
Day 60 mortality was numerically higher in the PCT group (30.0% vs 26.1%, difference 3.8%, 90% CI -2.1 to 9.7), with the upper CI boundary approaching the 10% non-inferiority margin.
Clinician overrides occurred frequently in both groups (overall non-adherence 45%), yet substantial separation in antibiotic duration was maintained.

outcomes_table.note: High event rates in both groups

outcomes_table.outcome: ICU length of stay from inclusion
outcomes_table.note: No reduction in length of stay
Largest separation seen in first episode duration

subgroup_table.subgroup: Duration of first episode: ventilator-associated pneumonia

safety: Day 28 all-cause mortality: 21.2% PCT vs 20.4% control (diff 0.8%, 90% CI -4.6 to 6.2)
Day 60 all-cause mortality: 30.0% PCT vs 26.1% control (diff 3.8%, 90% CI -2.1 to 9.7)
Day 28 SOFA score was statistically higher in the PCT-guided group (1.5 vs 0.9, P=0.0370)

domains.notes: Computer-generated allocation; stratified by centre with variable block sizes; allocation concealed prior to randomisation.
Open-label for treating clinicians and patients; potential performance bias offset by blinded expert adjudication committee for relapse and superinfection, and objective mortality measurement.
630 randomised, 9 excluded post-randomisation; 621 analysed in ITT population (307 PCT vs 314 control). 1 patient lost to follow-up per group for day 60 mortality.

High overall non-adherence (45%). PCT algorithm overridden in 219 episodes (including initiating antibiotics despite PCT <0.5 µg/L in 65 patients and continuing despite stop advice in unstable patients). Control group non-adherence occurred in 146 episodes (postponed initiation n=15, premature stopping n=46, continuation beyond guidance n=85).
Well balanced: age 64.4 vs 64.7 years; SAPS II 44.7 vs 42.6; day 1 SOFA 7.5 vs 7.2; septic shock 21.8% vs 18.5%; mechanical ventilation 78.5% vs 74.8%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate: causal inference for antibiotic reduction is supported, but open-label care, high clinician override rates (45%), and an imprecisely estimated 60-day mortality point estimate introduce risk of performance and implementation bias.

domains.notes: Adult ICU patients with suspected bacterial infection typical of general ICUs. Excluded very high acuity (SAPS II >65) and severely immunocompromised cohorts (AIDS, bone marrow transplant).
7 ICUs within France; requires rapid laboratory PCT turnaround (~2 hours) and a structured stewardship workflow. Reductions were largest where baseline treatment durations were longest.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate: applicable to general adult ICU populations with access to rapid PCT assays, but less generalizable to severely immunocompromised or extremely high-severity cohorts.

strengths: Pragmatic trial design evaluating a biomarker-guided discontinuation algorithm in a high-risk ICU cohort
Explicit PCT algorithm combined with rapid laboratory turnaround time (~2 hours)
Blinded expert committee adjudication of relapse and superinfection endpoints
Achieved clear separation in antibiotic exposure (-3.0 therapy days and +2.7 antibiotic-free days)
limitations: Open-label design susceptible to performance bias and co-interventions
High protocol deviation/override rates in both arms (45% overall) complicate algorithm-specific evaluation
Generous 10% non-inferiority mortality margin, with day 60 mortality point estimate numerically favoring control
Single-country setting where control clinicians received explicit protocol duration guidelines

critical_appraisal.summary: PRORATA provides moderate-certainty evidence that daily PCT guidance reduces ICU antibiotic duration, though open-label overrides and imprecise long-term mortality estimates warrant clinical caution.
strengths: Multicenter randomized design with rapid test turnaround
Blinded expert adjudication of secondary infectious events
Consistent reduction in antibiotic exposure across various infection sites

sections.authors_conclusion: A procalcitonin-guided strategy significantly reduced antibiotic exposure in ICU patients with suspected bacterial infection without compromising 28-day survival.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Procalcitonin serves effectively as an 'off-ramp' to shorten antibiotic durations in ICU patients rather than a trigger to withhold initial therapy.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: General adult ICU patients with suspected bacterial infection (respiratory, UTI, abdominal).
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean PCT should be used as a stand-alone test to withhold initial empiric antibiotics in unstable patients or septic shock.
implementation_caveats: Requires rapid lab turnaround (~2 hours) to influence daily clinician decisions
Algorithm permits and requires clinical overrides for unstable patients or high-risk syndromes
Effectiveness relies on shortening established therapy rather than preventing initial empiric doses

controversies.notes: A 10% absolute mortality margin is wide. Day 60 mortality numerically favored standard care (30.0% vs 26.1%) with the upper 90% CI reaching 9.7%, leaving potential safety concerns in high-risk subsets.

controversies.topic: Open-label stewardship and high override rates
controversies.notes: High override rates (45% overall non-adherence) mean the trial evaluates PCT as a decision-support guide within clinical discretion rather than strict algorithm efficacy.

context_related_trials.relation: Subsequent large multicentre ICU trial reproducing PCT-guided antibiotic duration reductions without excess mortality.

unresolved_questions: Safety and efficacy in patients excluded by design, such as SAPS II >65 or severely immunocompromised (AIDS, bone marrow transplant).
Whether PCT-guided reduction in antibiotic days directly leads to long-term reductions in hospital-acquired multidrug-resistant colonization.

numbers_to_remember: -3.0 days total antibiotic therapy (10.3 vs 13.3 days)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Daily procalcitonin safely shortens ICU antibiotic durations by ~3 days as a discontinuation tool, but clinical judgment must override low values in unstable patients.
